content: The term exogenous originates from the Greek words exo (meaning outside) and gen (meaning production). It describes an action or object that originates from outside a given system. This is in contrast to endogenous, which refers to something generated within the system. In biology, exogenous refers to any action or object that comes from outside a biological system. For instance, in medical imaging, an exogenous contrast agent is a liquid injected intravenously into a patient to enhance the visibility of a pathology, such as a tumor. An exogenous factor in biology is any material that is present and active within an organism or living cell but originates from outside that organism. This is distinct from endogenous factors, which are produced internally. Examples of exogenous factors in medicine include both pathogens and therapeutics. For example, DNA introduced into cells through transfection or viral infection (a process known as transduction) is considered an exogenous factor. Similarly, carcinogens, which are substances capable of causing cancer, are also classified as exogenous factors. In the field of attentional psychology, the term exogenous refers to attention being drawn involuntarily, without conscious intention. An example of this would be attention being captured by a flashing light in the peripheral field of vision.
